content: Cimetidine is a medication primarily used to treat and prevent ulcers in the stomach and intestines. It is also effective in managing conditions caused by excessive stomach acid, such as Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, erosive esophagitis, and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). By reducing stomach acid, it alleviates symptoms like stomach pain, heartburn, difficulty swallowing, coughing, and sleep disturbances. Cimetidine belongs to a class of drugs known as H2 blockers, which work by blocking H2 receptors in gastric parietal cells, thereby inhibiting gastric acid secretion. This medication is available both by prescription and over-the-counter. It can be used to treat occasional heartburn caused by acid indigestion or sour stomach and to prevent heartburn triggered by certain foods and beverages. When using cimetidine for self-treatment, it is important to follow the manufacturer’s instructions and consult a doctor or pharmacist if needed. Cimetidine is typically taken orally, and the dosage depends on the medical condition and response to treatment. For self-treatment of heartburn, one tablet is taken with water as needed, or 30 minutes before consuming food or drinks that may cause heartburn. Do not exceed two tablets in 24 hours unless directed by a doctor. For prescription use, it is important to take the medication regularly as prescribed, even if symptoms improve, to achieve the best results. Common side effects include headache, dizziness, drowsiness, and diarrhea. Rare but serious allergic reactions may occur. Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects such as confusion and pneumonia. During pregnancy, cimetidine should only be used when clearly needed, and it is not recommended during breastfeeding as it passes into breast milk. Cimetidine interacts with many medications by altering their metabolism, primarily through its inhibition of hepatic enzymes such as CYP1A2, CYP2D6, and CYP3A4. This can increase the levels or effects of certain drugs, potentially leading to adverse reactions. Examples of affected drugs include theophylline, warfarin, and certain antifungals. Additionally, cimetidine may reduce the absorption of medications that require an acidic environment, such as atazanavir and ketoconazole. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of all medications they are taking to avoid harmful interactions. Cimetidine is metabolized in the liver and has a bioavailability of 60-70%. It is minimally affected by first-pass metabolism and is partially protein-bound (15-20%). The drug and its inactive metabolites, such as cimetidine sulfoxide, are dialyzable. It can be administered via various routes, including oral, intramuscular, and intravenous, depending on the clinical situation. Lifestyle changes, such as stress reduction, smoking cessation, limiting alcohol intake, and dietary modifications (e.g., avoiding caffeine and spicy foods), can enhance the effectiveness of cimetidine. Regular medical and laboratory monitoring may be necessary during treatment. If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next scheduled dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. In cases of overdose, immediate medical attention is required. U.S. residents can contact the Poison Control Center at 1-800-222-1222, while Canadian residents can call 1-844-764-7669.
